title: How a Flea Circus Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of flea circuses, from the 1570s blacksmith Mark Scalliot's tiny flea-harnessed props through Louis Bertolotto's 1800s London shows, William Heckler's American flea circuses, and the methods used to harness, glue, and feed the fleas. They also cover the 1950s Michael Bentine-style "humbug" (fake) flea circuses using magnets and mechanisms, the Maria Fernanda Cardoso performance in the 1990s, and animal-cruelty objections. The episode closes with a listener mail from a teacher who uses the show in her classes.

segments.title: Google and Squarespace sponsor read and SketchFest promo
segments.summary: Sponsor read for Google and Squarespace offering a free trial and business email, followed by a promo for a Stuff You Should Know live show at SketchFest in San Francisco.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to flea circuses
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode, noting an earlier episode on fleas only briefly mentioned flea circuses, and describe flea circuses as cruel and older than the cartoon image most people have.

segments.title: Why fleas: jumping ability and early history
segments.summary: The hosts explain why fleas were chosen: they were ubiquitous and jump extremely well, storing energy in elastic cuticles in their legs. They recount the 1570s London blacksmith Mark Scalliot, reportedly the first to use a flea as a prop by fastening a tiny chain-like object to one.

segments.title: Louis Bertolotto and the first flea acts
segments.summary: Louis Bertolotto, an Italian impresario in London in the 1800s, is credited with making fleas the stars of shows. His acts included high-wire, sword fighting, historical reenactments such as Waterloo, soccer, high diving, and pulling chariots and carriages.

segments.title: Bertolotto's fame, disappearance and William Heckler in America
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Bertolotto's fame, a researcher reportedly found that he moved to Canada and lived anonymously, and early American flea master William Heckler, who reportedly earned large sums per day from performances.

segments.title: How flea acts were staged: harnessing, gluing and tricks
segments.summary: The hosts describe how fleas were tied with silk or gold wire nooses to props, that only about one in ten fleas were suitable, that props were glued to their legs, and how staged fights, soccer, juggling, and heat-driven dancing and music were created, with fleas' sensitivity to citronella and heat used to provoke movement.

segments.title: Costumed fleas, feeding fleas blood, and Heckler's later years
segments.summary: The hosts discuss costumed fleas made by Mexican nuns displayed in Cambridge, England, feeding fleas with the performers' own blood, and Heckler's flea circus in Times Square, which appeared in the film Easy Rider before being pushed out by peep shows.

segments.title: Humbug flea circuses and Michael Bentine's illusions
segments.summary: The hosts explain that some flea circuses used no real fleas, instead using stage magic called humbug flea circuses. George Tollerton wrote about them in the 1930s, and Michael Bentine performed an elaborate magnet-and-mechanism version on the Royal Variety Show in 1950. Tom Palmer's book The Famous Flea Act is mentioned.

segments.title: Modern revival, animal cruelty debate and wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts mention Maria Fernanda Cardoso's 1990s performance-art flea circus, objections from insect-cruelty societies calling for bans, and the difficulty of buying fleas today, noting a German flea circus at Munich Oktoberfest.

segments.title: Listener mail from a teacher
segments.summary: A listener who is a community college professor writes that the show has been a teaching tool, citing episodes on book banning, police interrogation, and hunting arguments, and asks for a shout-out to her sister Laura.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts thank the listener and give contact and website information.
